data.title: Huawei’s Tau Law Takes Commercial Form
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

In early September, Apple introduced the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone, marking the company’s entry into a smartphone segment that other manufacturers have been developing for several years. Huawei, Samsung, and others already have had foldable devices on the market, including tri-fold models.

The Huawei Mate XT 2 Ultimate Design tri-fold smartphone has made headlines not only for its large screen and tri-fold mechanism, inherited from the previous generation, but also for the new processor powering it.

Alongside the Mate XT 2, Huawei has introduced its Kirin 9050 Pro processor, referred to as “Kirin 2026” in earlier technical material. The processor implements Huawei’s Tau (τ) Scaling Law, introduced by He Tingbo, president of Huawei’s semiconductor unit, at the 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems.

With access to EUV lithography constrained, Huawei has developed a new chip design approach called LogicFolding. This technique stacks active silicon layers on top of each other, shortening signal paths and increasing transistor density.

From spatial geometry to temporal scaling

Because U.S. restrictions have blocked access to ASML’s EUV lithography equipment, Huawei has been seeking alternative ways to improve chip performance and density.

Conventional chip scaling, associated with Moore’s Law, has relied on shrinking transistor dimensions to increase transistor density. However, without advanced EUV lithography, thinner wires increase resistance and parasitic capacitance, which in turn slows the chip.

By focusing on how fast signals travel through the chip, LogicFolding addresses timing constraints. The technique improves digital, analog, and memory circuits across the stacked silicon layers by replacing long horizontal wires with short vertical connections. Huawei reported that this kind of vertical stacking reduces core routing lengths by 20% and shortens key timing paths by as much as 70%.

This new design also addresses heat issues. Because transferring data along horizontal wires accounts for more than 80% of a chip’s energy consumption, shorter signal paths reduce energy use. Huawei’s measurements, reported by TrendForce and EE Times China, indicate that power consumption fell by 66% for the neural processing unit, 58% for the graphics processing unit, and 41% for the CPU cores at comparable performance. To prevent the chip from overheating, Huawei has reduced operating voltages and clock speeds rather than increasing them.

Integrating 3D active layers presents formidable engineering and economic challenges. Mateo Valero, director of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), told EE Times that as silicon scaling hits physical boundaries, transistor-level innovation alone is insufficient. “The transistor is important, but what matters now is how an entire system behaves,” Valero said, emphasizing that success depends on full-stack orchestration. “You have to co-design from the application all the way down to the transistor, software, system-on-chip architecture, and memory layout, or you run into bottlenecks elsewhere.”

Consumer deployment and the global performance gap

The Huawei Mate XT 2 Ultimate Design, which is equipped with the new processor, is a tri-fold smartphone priced from 19,999 yuan (~$2,980) to 24,999 yuan (~$3,725). Sales began Sept. 12 and are currently limited to the Chinese market.

The chip features a nine-core CPU, with the primary core operating at 3.1 GHz, a Maleoon 920 GPU that supports hardware ray tracing up to 50 million rays per second, and a Da Vinci neural processing unit capable of running a 30-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts AI model directly on the device.

Manufacturing realities, foundry friction, and economic cost

Even with its new design, LogicFolding makes the manufacturing process much more complicated. SMIC has produced 7-nm-class chips without EUV lithography, and the Kirin 9050 Pro is believed to use a similar process, although Huawei has not disclosed the chip’s foundry or process node. The chip package incorporates two active layers and a 1.5-µm hybrid-bonding pitch, with approximately 50 million vertical connections, 10% to 15% of which carry active signals.

Huawei said its Kirin 2027 test silicon has already lowered the hybrid-bonding pitch to 1 µm, with more than 100 million vertical interconnects. Over the next three years, the company said it aims to achieve a pitch of 720 nm. By 2031, it targets a transistor density equivalent to a 1.4-nm process.

However, manufacturing yields suffer when active logic layers are connected directly. The process requires extremely accurate wafer thinning and smoothing to prevent small gaps, and misalignment of the copper pads can cause wiring problems and warping.

Addressing these hurdles, Valero observed that “unless memory arrangement, compilers, and hardware scheduling are seamlessly orchestrated, isolated architectural tricks cannot overcome physical manufacturing constraints.”

In the first half of 2026, Huawei’s R&D expenditure increased 25.2% year on year to 121.38 billion yuan (~$18.13 billion), equivalent to 25.9% of revenue. Meanwhile, net profit fell 36% to 23.81 billion yuan. U.S. export restrictions have forced Huawei to invest heavily in self-reliant AI and chip capabilities. Higher R&D costs, alongside rising memory chip prices, are continuing to weigh on the company’s overall profitability and consumer business.

LinxISA versus Arm and RISC-V

To protect its hardware from geopolitical risks, Huawei has moved away from standard instruction set architectures. Although the company holds a permanent license for the older Armv8 architecture, U.S. export laws still pose regulatory risks for using the newer Armv9 architecture.

To address these problems, Huawei is reportedly developing LinxISA, a block-structured instruction set architecture. Unlike Arm or RISC-V, which execute instructions one at a time, LinxISA executes instructions in blocks. Its use in the Kirin 9050 Pro has not been publicly confirmed.

Valero told EE Times that hardware decisions cannot be viewed in isolation, noting that optimizing individual hardware parts without full orchestration creates performance bottlenecks across the stack.

Software autonomy and enterprise compute ambitions

Huawei has released HarmonyOS 7, which doesn’t use any open-source Android code and relies on its own microkernel and EROFS file system.

Huawei said it intends to apply LogicFolding not just to its smartphones but also to its enterprise data centers and, by 2030, plans to launch the Ascend 990 AI chip to compete with Nvidia and Alibaba. On these end-to-end integration efforts, Valero remarked to EE Times that when architectural teams optimize “from top to bottom,” they can build systems “that claim to compete against Nvidia.”

Huawei is seeking to expand the domestic semiconductor equipment supply chain, alongside Chinese suppliers such as AMEC and NAURA, which are developing equipment for processes including etching, deposition, and advanced packaging. By bringing these different stages together, Huawei hopes to create a self-sufficient technology ecosystem for the development of advanced chips.

data.title: Delos Data Targets Heterogeneous AI With Data Interface
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

SANTA CLARA, Calif. – Delos Data is adding silicon to its portfolio, the startup announced at the AI Infra Summit. Delos previously announced data center orchestration software, Mosaic, and a new server architecture, Asterion, for huge scale-up domains, but is now working on Apollo, a data interface chiplet.

Apollo comes either as a 30+ Tbps I/O chiplet that sits next to an XPU, as a 10+ Tbps near-packaged optical interface, or on a 400+ Gbps card for CPUs and memory endpoints. It provides endpoints with guaranteed bandwidth and latency, handling load balancing, topology, and failure handling so the endpoint doesn’t have to do it. Delos is targeting order-of-magnitude improvements in speed, resiliency, and scale versus what endpoints can do today.  

The company also announced that it has raised more than $100 million in venture capital.

New AI infrastructure will cater to either regular inference, agentic AI, or both, Delos Data CTO Dan Daly told EE Times.

“The theme we see in these emerging new types of infrastructure buildouts is a mixture of hardware,” Daly said. “The CPU folks love to talk about how the CPU is back, but scale up and scale out only connects GPUs. There is another domain needed that includes GPUs, accelerators, CPUs, memory and storage. We’re offering a data interface that can bridge all these different types of devices, each with their own semantics, and put them in a single, flat, low-latency domain.”

For example, in prefill-decode disaggregated architectures, GPUs and dataflow accelerators have completely different approaches to memory, Daly said. GPUs place data in HBM and all compute units can access the data via the HBM’s memory map; it’s about data objects and addresses. In a dataflow architecture, a stream of data goes through a sequence of operations—the location determines what happens to the data. The semantics of these architectures are very different and need to be bridged.

Communication semantics can also be difficult, since a CPU and a memory controller (for example) may not speak the same language; today this is handled by a switch, but it incurs latency. It would be more efficient if interconnects could be aware of the semantics of both endpoints, Daly argues, and that is what Delos’ Apollo chiplet is designed to achieve.

“There’s an opportunity here to be able to greatly simplify the switching to really maximize the value of those switches—radix, latency, low power, flexibility of media—all the things you want from a switch and less of the things you don’t…legacy things from cloud or scale-out,” Daly said. “There’s an opportunity to open up the aperture here, to enable flexibility in terms of what switches go there, and to potentially simplify the network that goes in between these devices, where it could even be optical.”

Inference platforms may use copper and/or optical links, different types of switches, and different topologies, which require detailed co-design and customization. Delos does not want to replace switches; rather, it wants to add Apollo at each endpoint to reuse existing switches of any kind in a more efficient way.

Resiliency across multiple hops (that could mean bridging multiple types of semantics) is also critical.

“A lot of these devices were not born in this new environment, they were born on the board,” Daly said. “On the board, when you access memory or Flash, it always works. So the semantics of data memory expects that reads and writes always work. So we need to build in that assumption that even if a switch fails, it should still work.”

Delos’ data interface has to be in silicon because the lowest possible latency is required, Daly said. Apollo would replace today’s I/O chiplet in the package next to a multi-die GPU or XPU, or as a packaged chip on a board in near-packaged or co-packaged optics systems. There is also demand for a form factor resembling a traditional NIC, which can temporarily help bridge endpoints—particularly CPUs, which may not need the bandwidth but would benefit from latency improvements—into a cluster without requiring the Apollo chiplet, Delos CEO Ed Doe told EE Times.

“The common attribute across these [form factors] is latency, resiliency, and ultimately, the ability to bring [everything] in scale into a single domain,” Doe said.

Delos currently has an FPGA version of the card to offer, with NPO chips to appear next year, Doe said. The chiplet version is the same tapeout as the NPO chip version, but because of XPU design cycles, the chiptlet will not appear in XPU products for another couple of years, Doe said.  

Delos has also combined its hardware and software into a reference architecture and offers Morpheus, a development platform that bridges customers’ pre-silicon environments and lab environments to help customers co-design system topologies based on workloads and understand the impact of changes in connectivity.

Target customers for the Apollo chiplet include AI chip companies, such as hyperscalers and frontier labs working on their own silicon, Doe said.

According to the company, Delos’ Mosaic cluster management software is already deployed in production environments using customers’ existing infrastructure. The server, Asterion, will be sampling at the end of Q4. The development platform, Morpheus, is available now.

data.title: After IonQ Buyout, SkyWater Reiterates Role as Quantum Foundry
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

After quantum computing company IonQ acquired SkyWater in July this year, the subsidiary said it is pledging to treat its quantum chip customers equally, including parent IonQ.

“IonQ is treated as a customer of the foundry, just like anyone else,” SkyWater’s new SVP of quantum technologies Mihir Bhaskar told EE Times. “For all quantum customers SkyWater serves, their data and information remain strictly with the dedicated SkyWater team manufacturing their devices.”

Bhaskar, a quantum technologist for 15 years, founded Lightsynq, specializing in photonic interconnects and quantum memory, in 2024. IonQ acquired the company in 2025.

“Since joining IonQ, I’ve helped lead technology strategy, including assisting with the acquisition of SkyWater,” Bhaskar said. “With SkyWater now in place, the most exciting role for me is leading the SkyWater Quantum Solutions business unit to support all our quantum customers.”

SkyWater has nine “major” quantum customers, according to Bhaskar. Startup competitor Anderon has parent IBM as its primary customer and is looking for more.

“Priority number one for any business—especially in the foundry space—is protecting customer intellectual property,” Bhaskar said. “If your customers don’t trust you, you can’t do business. It is critical in the foundry business because customers bring highly sensitive IP and designs, trusting us to manufacture them.”

SkyWater has been making quantum chips for about 10 years. Its customers include IonQ, PsiQuantum, Qolab, and QuamCore.

Qolab and QuamCore are building what Bhaskar described as “potentially disruptive” superconducting technologies that may eliminate the well-known “chandelier” design from quantum computers.

“A major challenge in scaling superconducting qubit systems used by players like IBM, Google, and Rigetti is wiring and controlling larger numbers of qubits without creating a massive, tangled mess of cables,” Bhaskar said. “SkyWater is building a platform with Quadcore to solve these high-density integration and routing challenges.”

Modalities

The “modalities”, or techniques, that quantum chip companies use to make qubits include trapped ions, quantum dots, silicon vacancies in diamond, photonics, and superconducting.

Bhaskar said every one of those modalities ultimately relies on either superconducting or photonic methods to move quantum information.

“We support all major modalities,” Bhaskar said. “That might sound impossible for a single foundry, but fundamentally, there are only two ways to transport quantum information across a chip or system.”

SkyWater offers its SC250 (superconducting) and SP90 (photonics) platforms together with its technology-as-a-service model that provides early-stage process customization to prove manufacturability.

“While we offer baseline process design kit platforms [PDKs], our core business model accommodates custom process development within a volume manufacturing environment,” Bhaskar said. “We develop new processes outside standard PDKs to make breakthrough innovations manufacturable for the first time.”

Anderon

IBM established Anderon with the help of the U.S. government in May this year as the “world’s first” pure-play quantum chip foundry. The U.S. Department of Commerce awarded Anderon $1 billion under the CHIPS Act early in September to scale production. IBM is Anderon’s main customer.

Specific to the U.S., additional domestic capacity can help address supply chain constraints, provide manufacturing redundancy, and give quantum companies more options as they move from research prototypes toward production, Heather West, IDC’s quantum research lead, told EE Times.

Anderon offers customers wafers supporting superconducting qubit arrays, quantum input/output signaling, and readout signal chain components, new CEO Mukesh Khare told EE Times. The company plans to expand to other quantum modalities, such as spin qubits, he said.

“Fantastic step”

U.S. government investment in domestic quantum semiconductor manufacturing is a “fantastic step” for the entire ecosystem, Bhaskar said.

“Competitors like Anderon are building new 300-mm facilities for future capability,” Bhaskar noted.

SkyWater supplies its quantum customers from two 200-mm facilities in Minnesota and Florida as well as a 300-mm advanced packaging facility in Florida for chiplet integration and new materials.

“SkyWater is already shipping quantum wafers today and has been doing so for the last decade,” Bhaskar noted. “Our active capacity has powered the last several generations of quantum innovation and will continue to power the next. While others are working toward becoming a quantum foundry in the future, SkyWater is already the operational quantum foundry today.”

data.title: SEMICON India 2026: Startup Mitra Sheds Light on Early-Stage Silicon Startup Funding
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

At SEMICON India 2026, the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) held an early-stage silicon startup funding round under its Startup Mitra initiative, sponsored by Lam Research and Synopsys. Eleven startups were selected from a pool of 200, with Elphins Technologies taking first place, Meukron Technologies coming second, and Multi Nano Sense and CraftifAI jointly taking third. The top three received cash awards.

“We wanted to do a pitching event where the startups could raise funds,” said Akshay Agarwal, executive committee member at IESA and senior director of technology at MediaTek. He added that there was no commitment that the startups would receive funding from the VCs attending the event, but the organizers hoped the participants would be able to raise funds through connections made at the event.

From zero to one

The event targeted startups at the seed or pre-Series A stage, which the organizers described as the phase that takes a company “from zero to one.” The focus on early-stage funding comes as India’s semiconductor startups navigate the capital requirements of building products before they generate revenue.

Vishal Katariya, VP of deep science tech investing at Ankur Capital, told EE Times that the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme had helped de-risk seed rounds for many such companies.

“As a venture investor, if we are talking to a startup and we know that there is a good chance of it getting anywhere from ₹100 million [~$1.04 million] to ₹300 million [~$3.13 million] of support from the government, and if it is raising a comparatively sized seed round… there is a comfort that we receive,” Katariya said. “The risk profile of our investment is pushed down a little bit.”  He added that government support in some cases matches the size of the seed round itself.

Staircase capital

However, Katariya said the funding challenge extends beyond the seed round, with India needing more Series A, Series B, and other investors willing to back pre-revenue deep-tech companies. He said investors need to account for the value created as startups move through successive stages of technology development, rather than focusing only on revenue at an early stage.

He described this approach as “staircase capital”, reflecting how a startup’s technology moves from one technology readiness level to the next, with each stage adding value.

More than 20 venture capitalists attended Startup Mitra, along with other investors from the audience. The organizers said the event aimed to connect VCs with startups and with each other. It followed IESA’s earlier Startup Connect initiative at the Vision Summit, where startups pitched to Pontiac Ventures for connections and support rather than funding.

IESA executive committee member and India managing director for TYLSemi, Sundeep Gupta, said the organizing team received more than 70 applications through incubation centers across India. The applications were evaluated on technology, team, prototype level, intellectual property, and funding already received. “The selected startups spanned manufacturing, artificial intelligence, fabless semiconductor design, electronic design automation, defense, and automotive,” he said.

Navin Bishnoi, chairperson of IESA, outlined five Ts for startups: total addressable market, technology, team, timing, and treasure. He said IESA’s startup initiatives aim to help founders address these areas by providing access to capital, markets, policy, incentives, networks, and connections, with Startup Mitra focused particularly on capital.

Ajit Manocha, president and CEO of SEMI, called on VCs to support founders who had chosen to build startups over conventional employment, describing AI as accelerating innovation and startups as capable of turning difficult ideas into businesses. He urged VCs to back startups over the long term so founders could focus on developing their ideas.

Sudeep Shivalli, regional senior director at Synopsys India, highlighted the role of technology partners in helping startups develop products. For Startup Mitra, Synopsys committed $250,000 in credits for startups to access tools, storage, and licenses.

“We decided about $250,000 as a credit to enable the startups so that they can build the next product,” Shivalli said. “Today we are enabling globally more than 200 startups in this environment. We give them technology access; we give them compute, storage. In some cases, IPs are as well, so that we accelerate the entire product cycle.”

The support could help address some of the technology development costs faced by fabless semiconductor startups. Katariya said access to EDA tools, prototyping, and tape-out support can reduce financial barriers for companies at the early stage.

The six-member jury included Aadith Ramesh, associate at Peak XV Partners; Aashish Gupta of IvyCap Ventures; Abhishek Sud of Applied Ventures; Adarsh Sekhar, director at Lam Capital and Corporate Development at Lam Research India; Aviral Pandey, principal at AktiVentures; and Sunil Cavale, investment principal at Speciale Invest.

Katariya told EE Times that the seed-stage support provided by DLI has worked particularly well in the fabless space, where several beneficiaries have gone on to raise larger follow-on rounds. He cited Indian startups such as Mindgrove Technologies and NetraSemi as examples that raised $10 million or more in subsequent rounds, and said Ankur Capital’s own portfolio company, Turiyam AI, had drawn continued investor interest.

Katariya described deep-tech investing as requiring a different kind of underwriting than for typical startups, since investors back product creation rather than revenue creation at the stage firms like his come in.

Funding beyond tape-out

Katariya said the funding requirement can rise again as semiconductor startups move from tape-out toward commercial and high-volume production. “Companies still need capital for engineering work and volume production after the first chip and engineering samples, with the amount depending on the type of chip and potentially reaching the scale of an Indian Series B or Series C funding round,” he said.

He added that there is not yet any specific mechanism for Indian semiconductor startups to raise this production capital, leaving them to rely primarily on conventional equity funding. “The Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) fund could provide support to deep-tech startups through loans or equity,” he said.

Katariya expects Indian fabless companies to reach meaningful revenue once they move into volume production and sign purchase orders with customers. “Once that happens, you will see a good amount of investor interest,” he said. “Whenever there is one big success story, a lot of things will follow from that.”

data.title: SEMICON INDIA 2026: India Starts Packaging Chips as Ecosystem Takes Shape
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Twelve months ago, SEMICON India was about signatures on memoranda. At this year’s edition, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that India now has five chip assembly and packaging plants in commercial production and reiterated the commitment of $13.5 billion for the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0) to build out the ecosystem.

All five are back-end units, according to the government’s own count: assembly, test, marking and packaging (ATMP) lines, not wafer fabs. India’s first commercial fab, Tata Electronics’ 300-mm facility in Dholera, Gujarat, is still under construction. Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said ISM 2.0 is intended to go beyond individual plants and build design, equipment, materials, packaging, R&D, and talent capacity around them.

Modi virtually inaugurated two new production lines at the event—CDIL Semiconductor in Mohali, Punjab, for discrete devices, and Suchi Semicon in Surat, Gujarat, for packaging. They join Micron, Kaynes Semicon, and CG Semi among the 12 projects approved under the first phase. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said commercial DRAM and NAND production is now underway at its Sanand, Gujarat, plant. Suchi and eInfochips exchanged the first batch of commercial devices, described as India’s first commercial QFN chip.

Vaishnaw said, “The output is being exported…ATMP units are shipping to Japan, and [Indian-made] are also being incorporated into products exported to U.S. and EU countries such as Switzerland and Germany.”

Modi put ISM 2.0 at $13.5 billion, up from about $8 billion in the first phase. Separately, Vaishnaw said companies have made investment commitments of around ₹1 lakh crore (~$11–12 billion) under the ecosystem program, which he expects will create close to 100,000 jobs. He said these will materialize over two to three years as companies secure board and shareholder approvals.

That implies that, for now, these statements are commitments rather than spending.

Building beyond fabs

The ISM 2.0 program rests on six pillars: design, machines and materials, fabs, advanced packaging, applied R&D, and talent.

On design, the government is targeting 200 chip design startups. Of the 105 startups given access to EDA tools in the first phase, 20 have raised venture capital. About 70,000 design engineers have been trained in four years, against an original target of 85,000 over 10 years. Vaishnaw called the startup push “a game changer” for homegrown IP and said skilling will now move from chip design toward system design.

That push is taking place alongside an existing semiconductor engineering base in India that serves global customers. Ameer Saithu, EVP and global head of the Semiconductor Business Unit at HCLTech, told EE Times that the company handles semiconductor engineering from RTL through to post-silicon validation in India for global customers.

“Most of the capabilities that are required for spec to parts are in India,” Saithu said. “However, we also leverage a partnership ecosystem which is global, whether it is in the U.S., Taiwan, Malaysia, and Japan, and other places that come in as part of the partnership ecosystem.”

Saithu said India is also developing capabilities in areas that were previously concentrated elsewhere. He pointed to front-end design and HCLTech’s Advanced Semiconductor Lab in Bengaluru, which provides capabilities that companies previously accessed from Taiwan or Malaysia.

The expansion is not limited to chip design. Equipment and materials companies are also positioning themselves around the manufacturing projects now being built in India.

Applied Materials announced “India Vision 2035,” a $5 billion investment over the decade and a tenfold expansion of its India-based supply chain capacity. Lam Research said it will invest about ₹10,000 crore (~$1.05 billion) in its first silicon component and vertical ingot processing plant in India. Tokyo Electron plans a training center in Gujarat next year, and ASML said it is considering Indian suppliers for its global supply chain.

Tata Electronics signed MoUs with materials and gas suppliers including Fujifilm, JSR, Sumitomo Chemical, and INOX Air Products, plus one for a 363-acre vendor park at Dholera.

Its deal with Nexperia may be the most concrete on the fab side. Tata will lay the groundwork to make Nexperia’s MOSFET portfolio at Dholera and handle assembly and test of its discrete products at Jagiroad, Assam. Neither company disclosed volumes, timelines, or financial terms. Tata Electronics CEO Randhir Thakur said construction at both sites is on track; the company puts the combined investment at $14 billion.

AI drives custom silicon demand

Modi also framed the next phase of ISM 2.0 around AI-driven demand. He said the challenges now include “bringing memory closer to the processor, connecting many chips in such a way that they work together as one system, transferring huge amounts of data from here to there without delay, managing heat and power.” He also identified energy security as a major issue, noting that India’s installed solar capacity has grown “from about 2 gigawatts to more than 160 gigawatts.”

Saithu told EE Times that AI is contributing to a new wave of chip development, with demand coming not only from established semiconductor companies but also from companies that previously bought chips and now want to develop their own.

“In the AI area, there is a need for a wide variety of chips to be developed,” he said. “We are the partners that many of these customers come to for help in developing those chips.”

Saithu also pointed to companies specifically addressing the custom silicon market. “In all these areas, companies are having difficulty in time to market, which is our primary play. Either through our enhanced capabilities or through our solutions or AI-based acceleration of the silicon development lifecycle, we are able to deliver better time to market for our customers.”

The company has developed AI Force.Semi, a version of its AI Force platform aimed at the semiconductor value chain. Saithu said it covers work “from RTL to GDSII and post-silicon validation”, intending to use AI to reduce cycle time and effort and manage risk across the process.

That demand is developing alongside the wider expansion of India’s semiconductor ecosystem. The India Deep Tech Alliance, announced at last year’s SEMICON India with $1 billion in venture capital backing, has reported $263 million invested across 56 companies. Vaishnaw also revealed that an unnamed fab scheduled to start production in 2028 has already booked a large share of its capacity. A year ago, the Union Minister hinted at ISM 2.0 while citing 10 approved projects. That number is now 12, with five already in production.

Expanding India’s chip development capabilities

The expansion is also creating demand for capabilities further along the semiconductor development cycle. Engineering, testing, equipment, materials, training, and R&D are being built around the manufacturing projects, while companies are also expanding capabilities that previously required access to facilities outside India.

HCLTech’s Advanced Semiconductor Lab in Bengaluru is one example. The company has invested about ₹185 crore (~$19.3 million) in the facility, which supports prototyping and new product introduction (NPI), including silicon characterization, validation, and reliability testing from wafer to system level.

“It is a real production lab where it is integrated into the engineering process,” Saithu said. “We are currently using it to actually deliver chips in the market.”

The facility is used for engineering and R&D, including sample volume testing before chips move to volume production. Saithu said it had been operational for a few weeks at the time of the interview, with customers already onboarded and further space and capabilities still being ramped up.

HCLTech had previously provided similar services in collaboration with partners and used capabilities in locations such as Taiwan and Malaysia. “Now we have it in India, and that collapses cycle times,” Saithu said. “That helps us meet our customers’ time-to-market requirements in a much better manner.”

He said the facility can also help startups that might otherwise face higher costs and logistical difficulties when accessing these services outside India.

Talent is another part of the build-out. Saithu said HCLTech has established training programs and works with universities in India to develop curricula, mentor students, and recruit from those programs.

He said India’s next area of development is product management and systems-level thinking in silicon. “The front end, especially the initial parts of the design, we are there, but we could be scaling much more,” he said.

The three-day SEMICON India event at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi brought together more than 600 companies from 52 countries. The event recorded 51,656 total registrations and cumulative footfall of about 40,000 over the three days. Organizers counted 41 MoUs and announcements during the first two days, followed by 15 more at the closing session on Sept. 19.

data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Novigrad founders Christopher Elash and Lars Kishchuk set out to make chips. Conversations within Canada’s semiconductor industry, however, led them to a more pressing opportunity: addressing a gap in the country’s ecosystem, which ultimately gave rise to the inception of the Saskatoon-based startup.

The two University of Saskatchewan engineering graduates, who previously worked together on university space projects such as Saskatchewan’s first satellite initiative, discovered that many companies developing electronics for space applications faced a common challenge: Radiation qualification and testing, essential for electronics operating in space and other harsh environments, was often costly, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on facilities outside Canada.

“We should make chips; everyone loves making chips,” Elash said in an interview with EE Times. But companies kept telling him that doing radiation testing is “just awful,” and they’re behind schedule, he said.

The founders also discovered that Canada’s space sector was larger and more active than they had anticipated. Companies developing everything from communications hardware and power electronics to memory devices and processing systems were seeking domestic support for radiation testing and qualification.

Many had previously relied on U.S. providers, but Novigrad has found there are more than enough customers at home to keep the company busy. “We knew that there was a bit of a market here,” Kishchuk said. “Every week or two, we get reached out to by a different entity in Canada.”

The work spans a wide range of devices. Memory components such as SRAM, RAM, and flash remain common candidates for testing, particularly as “new space” companies seek to qualify components for orbital applications.

Novigrad’s founders said there is no single dominant category. Projects can involve power systems, signal processing hardware, communications electronics, or custom integrated devices. “That’s the fun part,” Elash said. “There isn’t really any common device.” The company sees everything from power amplifiers and memory components to processing and communications electronics.

In a recent webinar hosted by Canada’s Semiconductor Council, Elash outlined how many organizations want to use commercial off-the-shelf components in space but first need confidence that those devices can withstand radiation exposure and continue to operate as intended.

He said a major focus of Novigrad’s work is testing for radiation-induced failures, particularly single-event effects. These occur when individual particles strike a semiconductor device and cause temporary faults such as bit flips, voltage transients, or software crashes. “This is the concern that keeps people up at night,” Elash said.

Novigrad also evaluates cumulative radiation damage through prolonged exposure testing. Using cobalt-60 gamma sources, engineers assess how devices degrade over time, tracking effects such as increased leakage currents, reduced speed, and changes in operating characteristics.

To recreate real-world conditions, the company employs radiation chambers, laser-based systems, and particle accelerator facilities. “We recreate the environment that it’d be operating in, in some sort of accelerated and controlled setting on the ground,” Elash said. The resulting data is then translated into engineering recommendations, providing customers with a clearer understanding of device reliability before deployment.

Space applications are the primary driver of Novigrad’s business, but the company sees growing interest in defense and Arctic applications, where radiation effects are not always fully understood. Electronics operating in northern regions can encounter elevated radiation exposure because Earth’s magnetic field channels charged particles toward the poles.

Kishchuk said that as Canada invests more in northern surveillance and sovereignty capabilities, understanding that environment becomes increasingly important.

Novigrad is also exploring opportunities with other Canadian facilities, including the Saskatchewan Cyclotron Centre, and investigating how advanced laser-based fault-injection systems developed at the university could serve as a lower-cost pre-screening alternative before customers commit to scarce accelerator beam time.

Canada has strong research infrastructure to support radiation testing and space qualification, including the testing capabilities of TRIUMF in British Columbia. The University of Saskatchewan in Novigrad’s home city hosts the Semiconductor Technology And Rad-Effects Research Lab.

Both founders believe the country possesses the talent needed to build a stronger radiation-effects ecosystem. “A few years ago, people thought they couldn’t do this work in Canada,” Elash said. “Now they’re looking to come back home and bring all the experience and knowledge.”

As commercial and government launch activity continues to expand, demand for radiation-hardened semiconductors grows. Each new satellite, payload, and orbital computing platform requires components that can withstand cumulative radiation exposure and single-event effects without sacrificing performance or mission life.

In early 2026, NHanced Semiconductors announced it had chosen Avalanche Technology’s MRAM for its FPGA targeting satellite and defense applications after other evaluated options failed to meet the requirements of its radiation-hardened FPGA system-in-package integration, including dependable standby capability and high-confidence operational performance.

In summer 2025, Micron Technology introduced a high-density, radiation-tolerant single-level cell NAND product with a die capacity of 256 gigabits—the first in a portfolio that will include space-qualified NAND, NOR, and DRAM solutions.

More recently, Infineon Technologies’ radiation-hardened HiRel power devices were launched into space aboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Meanwhile, SpaceX is targeting late 2027 for orbital data centers, which will need to account for radiation exposure.

data.title: AI Power Demands Push GaN into Data Center Design
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The rapid increase in AI computing performance is forcing a fundamental redesign of data center power architectures, with gallium nitride (GaN) emerging as a key technology for meeting the industry’s escalating efficiency and power density requirements.

Speaking at the recent EE Power Asia 2026 Spark Session, Alex Lidow, CEO of Efficient Power Conversion (EPC), and Jason Zhang, VP of DC/DC marketing and system engineering at EPC, outlined why conventional silicon power devices are approaching their practical limits as GPU power consumption continues to climb.

According to Zhang, AI accelerators have experienced a fourfold increase in power consumption across three GPU generations. Within the next two years, individual GPUs are expected to dissipate as much as 5 kW while operating at core voltages below 1 V, requiring current levels approaching 10,000 A.

“When you have hundreds or thousands of GPUs in one data center, the data center scales toward a gigawatt,” Zhang said.

Meeting those requirements requires multiple stages of power conversion, from 480-V three-phase AC to an 800-V DC bus, followed by intermediate voltages such as 12 V or 6 V before reaching the GPU core voltage. Each conversion stage must deliver extremely high current while minimizing losses and occupying as little board space as possible.

AI architectures driving power redesign

The transition to AI infrastructure is also changing how power is distributed inside hyperscale servers.

Lidow said conventional architectures that brought AC power directly into server racks are giving way to centralized sidecar power systems that deliver an 800-V DC bus into each rack. Power conversion then occurs directly on the server board, eliminating bulky power supply drawers while reducing distribution losses.

“The rack now is receiving 800 V instead of AC, and it needs to break it down to eventually 0.7, 0.6 or 0.5 V for the GPU,” Lidow explained.

Although higher distribution voltage reduces current flowing into the server, the final conversion stages must still supply thousands of amperes to modern AI processors. This places enormous pressure on power converters to achieve both high efficiency and high current density.

Lidow described server board space as “the most expensive real estate in the world,” making power density as important as efficiency. Higher switching frequencies reduce the size of magnetic components, allowing more power conversion circuitry to fit within the limited space surrounding AI processors.

Silicon approaches its limits

Both speakers argued that silicon MOSFET technology has largely reached its performance ceiling for next-generation AI systems.

Zhang noted that silicon has steadily improved over the years but is now approaching its theoretical limit in terms of on-resistance. Incremental improvements have become increasingly difficult while AI power requirements continue to accelerate.

“Each generation improves only around 20%,” Zhang said. “It’s just not enough. They cannot keep up with the sheer speed of the power requirement.”

GaN devices, by comparison, continue to improve rapidly. EPC’s seventh-generation platform introduces lower on-resistance and lower gate charge across both higher-voltage devices and a new family of low-voltage products ranging from 18 V to 40 V, targeting the multiple conversion stages inside AI servers.

Lower gate charge enables higher switching frequencies, reducing the size of passive components while increasing overall power density.

Zhang added that EPC’s Gen 7 devices are capable of switching efficiently at about 3 MHz in synchronous buck converters, roughly 3× the switching frequency typically achieved by comparable silicon implementations.

The company’s roadmap targets switching frequencies approaching 10 MHz, enabling current densities of roughly 5 A/mm² for future AI processors requiring 10,000 A of current.

GaN expands throughout the server

Lidow expects GaN to be deployed across virtually every power conversion stage inside future AI servers.

Today, GaN is already widely used in the 48-V input stage. As AI architectures migrate toward 800-V distribution and lower intermediate voltages, GaN is being designed into additional conversion stages, including 800-V input converters, intermediate bus converters, and point-of-load regulators.

“GaN is everywhere on the server card, and silicon no longer can meet these requirements,” Lidow said.

He explained that lower-voltage conversion stages require substantially more semiconductor area because current increases as voltage decreases. Consequently, GaN adoption is expected to accelerate as power conversion moves closer to the GPU.

“It’s almost like a wave of GaN going across that server card right now,” Lidow said.

Scaling manufacturing and ensuring reliability

One concern surrounding widespread GaN deployment has been manufacturing capacity. Zhang argued that this is no longer a limiting factor.

Unlike silicon carbide (SiC), GaN devices are produced on silicon substrates using largely conventional silicon manufacturing equipment, supplemented by epitaxial growth processes. EPC also relies on multiple ecosystem partners for wafer fabrication, testing, packaging, and logistics.

“The good thing about GaN is that GaN has no capacity constraint,” Zhang said.

Reliability has also evolved significantly over nearly two decades of development.

Rather than relying solely on traditional silicon qualification methods, EPC evaluates GaN devices within their intended applications, identifies intrinsic failure mechanisms, and modifies device design and manufacturing processes to eliminate them.

“The major variation variable in terms of field reliability is how the part is used and the customer side,” Zhang said, noting that thermal interfaces, PCB mounting, and heatsink attachment have become more significant factors than intrinsic device reliability.

Lidow added that EPC’s GaN devices have already accumulated eight years of deployment on AI data center cards with “phenomenal reliability.”

Meanwhile, beyond improving GPU power delivery, both executives argued that GaN plays a growing role in reducing overall data center operating costs.

Zhang noted that hyperscale operators increasingly evaluate total facility efficiency rather than only processor performance. Even modest improvements in conversion efficiency can significantly reduce electricity consumption, cooling requirements and water usage across gigawatt-scale AI facilities.

“GaN can easily improve overall efficiency by 5% from AC to the core,” Zhang said. “The 5% is a lot in terms of operating costs.”

He also expects environmental considerations to become increasingly important as AI infrastructure expands, particularly in regions where electricity consumption, water usage and community impact are receiving greater regulatory scrutiny.

What’s next

Looking ahead, Lidow expects AI power architectures to continue evolving toward higher distribution voltages and lower intermediate bus voltages.

While 800-V distribution is becoming the industry baseline, future GPU generations may require 1,200-V, 1,500-V or even 2,000-V primary buses, supported by multilevel converter topologies, he said. Intermediate buses are expected to move from 12 V toward 6 V before direct GaN conversion to sub-1 V GPU core supplies.

Within EPC, future development is shifting away from discrete transistors toward increasingly integrated GaN power ICs.

“I think we have squeezed all that we can out of GaN discretes,” Lidow said. “Going forward, I think all of our developments are going to be ICs.”

He believes integration will become necessary as switching speeds continue to increase, enabling distributed gate drivers, monolithic power stages, and higher levels of functionality that cannot be achieved with discrete components alone.

Lidow concluded that GaN will continue expanding its role inside AI servers as compute requirements increase.

“It is clear that in the world of servers, GaN will dominate the server card,” he said. “I think we will get every single power socket on there.”

The NAND flash market is likely to have a new player, and it’s from China. ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), which has already shaken up the DRAM market, is reportedly preparing to enter NAND flash to capitalize on a global memory shortage driven by surging demand from AI servers. Data centers need more solid-state drives (SSDs)—built around NAND flash—to store AI workloads.

According to Reuters, the company is setting up an R&D production line for NAND chips at its new fab in Beijing. Moreover, CXMT has established a research institute in Beijing, where projects include the development of NAND flash technology. Reuters also quoted an unnamed startup in China that is currently in talks with CXMT to use its NAND chips in storage products for AI systems and supercomputers.

First and foremost, it’s noteworthy because CXMT is moving beyond its core DRAM business. China’s twin memory stars, CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp. (YMTC), have so far operated strategically in two major memory segments: CXMT is China’s largest DRAM manufacturer, and YMTC leads the NAND market in China.

However, in April this year, Reuters reported that YMTC had sent low-power DRAM samples to customers as it weighed entry into CXMT’s core market. YMTC expects customer feedback by the end of 2026, which will help it decide whether to start DRAM production. Now CXMT is considering a foray into the NAND flash market.

On the surface, it may seem that CXMT and YMTC are readying to move into each other’s memory turf. However, both CXMT and YMTC are backed by China’s national semiconductor fund and local governments. CXMT grew with ⁠backing from Hefei, the provincial capital of Anhui province in eastern China; YMTC expanded with backing from Wuhan, the provincial capital of central Hubei province.

A flash window of opportunity

A closer look at CXMT and YMTC encroaching on each other’s memory territories shows it’s about more than sparking direct competition in China’s domestic market. CXMT’s entry into NAND could inevitably generate friction over domestic equipment distribution, cleanroom tooling quotas, and specialized engineering talent from regional institutions. However, it also eliminates single-supplier vulnerabilities for memory consumers in China.

Memory industry leaders Samsung and SK Hynix have maintained commanding positions across both DRAM and NAND markets, and Micron has followed suit, though it initially lagged in NAND flash. The dual-memory portfolio allows chipmakers such as Samsung to absorb market downturns by continuously shifting capital between DRAM and NAND operations.

Both CXMT and YMTC likely want to become one-stop shops for DRAM and NAND, just like their bigger rivals Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix. The timing couldn’t be better, amid a global memory shortage driven by AI server demand that industry executives expect to persist through at least 2027.

Both CXMT and YMTC could gain global market share by competing aggressively on price as memory supplies remain tight. However, according to the Korean newspaper Chosun Ilbo, that represents a longer-term competitive threat for global rivals rather than an immediate supply response.

At a time when the memory troika—Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix—has prioritized capital spending on DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), limiting additions to NAND flash capacity and worsening shortages in this segment mark a window of opportunity for China’s largest memory chipmaker.

But the question is: How viable is this move? CXMT has neither announced a full commercial capacity target nor a publicly detailed production timetable.

Can CXMT pull it off?

Apparently, CXMT’s NAND plan is a work in progress. NAND flash is among the most capital-intensive undertakings in the semiconductor industry. It requires distinct tooling configurations and chemical supply chains, as well as completely different patent architectures compared to DRAM.

NAND manufacturing entails specialized process technology, production equipment, quality controls, and long-term design validation. Therefore, moving from an R&D line to commercially competitive volume production would involve substantial technical and financial challenges.

While the company is awash in cash after a blockbuster IPO, access to advanced chipmaking tools still poses significant challenges amid U.S. export controls. On the technical front, the shift from DRAM fabrication to vertical 3D NAND manufacturing creates steep operational challenges. DRAM relies on precise lateral photolithography to pattern dense capacitor networks at tiny dimensions, while 3D NAND devices are manufactured vertically.

So, CXMT, which spent the past decade developing a competitive DRAM technology, will most likely spend the next decade expanding beyond DRAM and into the NAND flash realm. This strategic expansion into flash memory also marks an inflection point in mainland China’s broader campaign to solidify semiconductor self-reliance across critical supply chains.

data.title: AI, Crypto Mining Expose Global Compute Infrastructure Constraints
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

BARCELONA, Spain — At the 12th European Blockchain Convention, institutional investors and technology executives discussed the growing infrastructure needs of digital assets. Against that backdrop, AI workloads, specialized mining hardware, semiconductor constraints, and energy availability are putting pressure on global compute infrastructure.

In an interview with EE Times, Victor Teixeira, chief investment officer at General Tensor, explained how semiconductor supply and energy grid limitations affect digital compute, with Europe at the center of the squeeze.

Geopolitical pressures and European supply limits

Teixeira, whose background includes mergers and acquisitions in the energy sector across Europe and Australia, pointed to historical policy decisions as a root cause of Europe’s current vulnerability.

He said that, as de-industrialization took hold, European policymakers shut down domestic coal-fired power stations on the assumption that industrial capacity could be transferred to manufacturing centers in China, Vietnam, and other developing countries.

He argued that this approach has broken down because of two geopolitical forces. On the one hand, U.S. industrial policy has reoriented supply chains toward domestic priorities. On the other, he said, China has deliberately addressed its domestic manufacturing bottlenecks to retain control of its key supply networks.

“As far as Europe is concerned, we are now in a situation in which we are entirely supply constrained,” Teixeira stated. “We lack the manufacturing facilities, we don’t have the natural resources necessary for manufacturing, and our supply chains are not tough enough to protect themselves against such a situation.”

The economy’s recovery after the pandemic revealed the fragility of the system, he said. Semiconductor manufacturing fabs can take five to seven years to go from construction to production, while leading foundries allocate capacity two or three years in advance.  As a result, Europe faces persistent constraints on hardware availability. At the same time, its power infrastructure limits efforts to expand digital capacity.

ASICs versus GPUs

The computing landscape is becoming more specialized as processing architectures evolve. In the past, GPUs—originally designed for video games—provided essential hardware for early Bitcoin mining and AI models because of their flexible, general-purpose computing capabilities.

“Video games are to tech what Formula 1 is to cars—it is always the hardest, weirdest solutions that come out of video games,” Teixeira noted.

As mining difficulty increased, Bitcoin mining shifted from GPUs to ASICs, devices designed to execute a specific cryptographic algorithm efficiently by removing unnecessary graphics pipelines and operating system overhead.

Teixeira compared this hardware optimization to traditional software engineering, noting how developers on the PlayStation 1 reduced system memory allocations to free up performance for more demanding programs.

A similar architectural split is happening in AI. Although Nvidia and AMD provide general-purpose GPUs to large-scale data centers, specialized AI ASICs are emerging from China. These purpose-built chips have eliminated older GPU features to focus entirely on AI inference and training.

As Teixeira explained, “Bitcoin ASICs are not suitable for carrying out AI workloads, but GPUs can handle both. There comes a stage when you end up splitting the work, with some tasks using one type of equipment and others using another.” GPUs will remain useful for a range of workloads, but Teixeira expects specialized hardware will gradually take over most high-volume operations.

Foundry bottlenecks and supply chain

The struggle over access to advanced semiconductor nodes has now become a key strategic arena. Cutting-edge processor production depends heavily on TSMC, intensifying competition among AI developers, cloud providers, and hardware designers.

Companies with less ability to absorb high chip costs are being pushed away from leading-edge production. For instance, automotive manufacturers mainly rely on mature nodes—28-nm and above. Yet achieving very high energy efficiency can require advanced process geometries, such as 3-nm process technology.

This is evident in recent ASIC developments. Japanese company Triple-1 taped out its third-generation Bitcoin-mining chip, the Kamikaze III, on TSMC’s 3-nm process. The chip aims to achieve an energy efficiency of 10.45 joules per terahash by operating at sub-threshold voltages of 0.26 volts. The company argued that its Japanese base gives it an advantage over Chinese developers that are restricted from accessing advanced nodes.

Energy infrastructure and coin per watt

Beyond silicon fabrication, energy infrastructure is a major operational constraint. In the U.S., data centers usually draw power from regional grids or independent generation in unregulated markets such as Texas. By contrast, in Europe, much of the power grid infrastructure was established in the mid-20th century and lacks the interconnections needed to accommodate rapidly growing data center loads.

In the U.K., operators frequently curtail large amounts of wind power capacity. “Many wind farms are dumping 40% of the electricity they produce since they are unable to sell it on to the grid,” Teixeira said.

Because of these grid limitations, crypto mining and AI data centers have to differ in how they assess location and power costs. As Teixeira pointed out, crypto mining operations tend to move toward the lowest-cost power sources, such as stranded hydroelectric power in the Nordic countries or excess renewable energy output. Worldwide, crypto mining represents 183 TWh of power capacity (Dec. 2024), roughly 30% to 40% the entire data center industry’s power footprint, at the time.

Teixeira stressed that the basic economic incentives that govern crypto mining and AI are quite different. “As for Bitcoin, I mine it, then sell the Bitcoin—you have to achieve profitability right away, because if you don’t, you’re in effect paying just to mine and ending up with nothing,” Teixeira said. “With regard to AI, currently a great deal of it is operating at a loss when selling the product, on the basis that future revenue will be so large as to offset the loss incurred today.”

With energy costs rising, infrastructure providers are exploring modular power options, such as small nuclear reactors and biomass generation, located next to their data centers.

data.title: Intel Puts High-NA EUV into Production, but Stitching Still Has Something to Prove
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Intel Foundry has moved ASML’s high numerical aperture (High-NA) EUV lithography into production, but the harder problem of stitching together larger chip designs is still working its way toward high-volume manufacturing.

Intel said High NA has now been used on more than one million wafers across tool certification, R&D, and production, including select layers of a subset of Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors, code-named Panther Lake. The company said overlay, throughput, and availability are meeting expectations, while the High-NA-patterned Intel 18A layers deliver yield, defectivity, electrical performance, and reliability comparable with layers patterned using conventional 0.33-NA EUV.

But Panther Lake does not prove that the industry has solved the most difficult stitching problems. The layers patterned with High NA were deliberately selected so that no electrical connections needed to cross the boundary between the two half-fields. The goal was to demonstrate that High NA could operate inside a real production flow and to gain manufacturing experience without changing the performance of the finished product.

That distinction matters because the basic optics of High NA create a new field-size problem.

Why High NA needs stitching

Conventional 0.33-NA EUV can expose a 26 mm × 33 mm field using a standard 6×6-inch mask. High NA increases the numerical aperture to 0.55, improving resolution, but its anamorphic optics cut the exposure field in half, to 26 mm × 16.5 mm. Designs that fit inside that half-field pose no problem. Larger designs require either two exposures that are stitched together or, eventually, a larger mask.

The problem is becoming more important as advanced chips get larger. “The need for stitching has only grown,” Chris Mack, co-founder and CTO of Fractilia, a lithography metrology software company, told EE Times. AI accelerators and other large chips are increasingly filling a conventional reticle field, he said, making full-field High-NA patterning more desirable.

Intel Foundry is pursuing several ways to make that possible. The simplest case is to avoid electrically significant crossings at the seam altogether, as Intel did on Panther Lake. A more flexible approach is block-and-route stitching, in which designers place the seam so that critical standard-cell circuitry does not cross it and route connections through higher metal layers instead.

Mark Phillips, distinguished engineer at Intel Foundry, described block-and-route as one step in a broader strategy for using today’s 6-inch masks with High NA. Intel is also developing what it calls two-dimensional, or “Zipzag,” stitching, in which the seam can move around sensitive circuitry or IP blocks instead of running in a straight line.

The name evokes the zigzag stitch used in sewing. Rather than forcing the boundary between the two High-NA exposures to follow a straight line across the die, Zipzag allows the seam to jog around sensitive regions of the design. That gives chip designers more freedom to keep critical circuitry away from the stitching boundary, although it also adds complexity to mask construction, inspection, and manufacturing control.

Electrical proof comes in stages

Intel has already electrically verified block-and-route on a full-loop test chip with a straight-line seam. The test structures compare the resistance and variation of metal lines crossing the stitching boundary with control structures that don’t cross it, while additional chains and combs check for shorts and opens.

The latest Zipzag test chip goes further. It includes electrical test structures spanning a jogged seam. Inline imaging, overlay, and defect measurements indicate that the jogged regions are healthy, but electrical test results are still pending.

Mack sees block-and-route as relatively low risk. “It seems relatively straightforward, it seems low risk, and it looks like that is the path that everyone will try for their first stitching exercises,” he said.

The harder case is feature stitching, where critical features themselves cross the boundary between two exposures. That requires much tighter control over how the two patterns overlap.

“What we’re talking about is making the technology ready for high-volume manufacturing,” Mack said. At that point, the problem becomes more than just overlay. Dose, focus, edge placement, and stochastic variation all matter.

The seam has to survive statistical tails

Mack said stitching errors of interest can be only a few nanometers, while stochastic edge roughness can also be on the order of a few nanometers. Manufacturers therefore have to distinguish systematic errors caused by stitching from random variation already present in the lithography process.

That challenge is compounded by metrology itself. Scanning electron microscopes, the workhorse for measuring these features, introduce image noise that can resemble real stochastic variation on the wafer. Fractilia is working with Intel on methods to separate those effects and measure systematic stitching errors.

Average results alone may not be enough. Mack said rare failures in the long tails of statistical distributions can emerge at parts-per-million or even parts-per-billion levels. A stitching process that looks healthy on average can therefore still create yield problems once millions of devices are being manufactured.

That’s why yield ultimately matters more than a clean demonstration. “Yield is the big unknown until you actually run the experiments,” Mack said.

The same uncertainty complicates the economic comparison between High NA and continued multi-patterning with 0.33-NA EUV. Engineers can model the cost of one High-NA exposure against two, three, or four lower-NA exposures, but the calculation can change substantially if one approach produces better yield.

Intel’s Panther Lake experiment was not intended to demonstrate such an economic advantage. The High-NA step replaced a 0.33-NA step in a way designed to leave the finished product unchanged. The exercise was primarily about production readiness and learning how the tools behave under real manufacturing loads.

Larger masks could remove the seam

Stitching may eventually become unnecessary. Intel and ASML are pushing the industry toward larger 6×12-inch masks. A mask twice as large in one dimension would allow a High-NA scanner to expose a full conventional reticle field without stitching. Intel said the larger format could also improve productivity on 0.33-NA EUV tools by combining what would otherwise require two 6-inch masks.

Mack said he believes stitching will work, but ultimately, he sees the larger mask as the preferable solution. “The productivity improvements that come from using a 6×12 mask alone will justify its use,” he said.

The transition will not happen quickly. Based on discussions at the SPIE Photomask Technology + Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography conference in Monterey in early September, Mack said the industry appears to be coalescing around the larger-mask direction, but he heard timelines of roughly five years to first mask demonstrations and seven years before those masks could be used to print wafers.

That leaves stitching with an important role for years to come. Intel has demonstrated that High NA itself can operate in production. The next challenge is making stitching sufficiently predictable, measurable, and easy to design around so that customers can use the smaller High-NA field without compromising yield.

The optics are already in the fab. The harder task now is making everything around them routine.

//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The seemingly unending surge in AI infrastructure spending will continue to create DRAM supply shortages, which industry analysts believe could persist well into 2027 and potentially beyond.

This latest cycle differs significantly from previous DRAM booms and busts, when memory demand was tied largely to PCs and smartphones. AI has made memory a critical component of data center infrastructure, leading to more acute and long-lasting supply constraints.

“This is the most undersupplied the DRAM market has been in decades,” Mike Howard, director of DRAM and memory markets at TechInsights, said in an interview with EE Times, adding that pricing and revenue growth have surged as AI deployments accelerate. He expects supply constraints to continue through 2027 because demand growth is exceeding the industry’s ability to add manufacturing capacity.

Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, shares a similar view. “I don’t see how markets really loosen up anytime soon,” he said in an interview with EE Times. “Everybody knows that the capacity that comes in next year seems to be fully committed, so I don’t see a scenario where you have excess supply in the next 18 months.”

Despite the high demand, memory makers are exercising discipline. Rather than overbuilding capacity as they have in previous cycles—which ultimately led to significant oversupply and collapsing prices—they are taking a more measured approach. “They’ve been very methodical and very careful to spend money because of what’s happened cycle after cycle,” Gastwirth said.

He pointed to long-term agreements and customer-funded expansion plans as evidence that producers are growing capacity with considerably less risk than in the past.

Howard also sees structural changes reducing the likelihood of a classic memory crash. Long-term supply agreements now cover a significant portion of industry output, helping suppliers better align production with demand and avoid large inventory accumulations.

What remains to be seen is whether the current AI demand can remain strong enough over the longer term to justify continued expansion and whether the AI bubble is on the verge of popping.

Both Howard and Gastwirth expect the long-term trajectory to maintain its course, regardless of any setbacks. “There is real concern about an AI bust, and it is warranted,” Howard said. However, the economic promise of AI and the need for increasingly capable computing systems support ongoing investment, he said.

Gastwirth said he doesn’t believe there will be an AI bust given all the benefits that have already been seen from LLMs alone. He acknowledged uncertainty around issues such as job displacement and adoption timelines, but he believes AI’s impact is already too significant to reverse.

Beyond training and inference workloads, Gastwirth sees robotics and physical AI as the next major driver of memory demand. “When you get the robotics really starting to pick up, you need duplicate and triplicate systems for robots to really work.” He said the amount of information that’s gathered with all the sensors will require exponentially more DRAM.

Gastwirth said the resulting data growth from physical AI could create new demand streams that extend the current memory cycle well beyond today’s data center buildouts.

“Memory has become one of the most important components in the AI hardware stack, often the gating semiconductor component,” Howard said, arguing that memory now serves as a bottleneck for system deployment rather than a supporting element.

The consequences are already being felt outside the AI market. With hyperscale customers willing to pay premium prices for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM, consumer electronics makers find themselves lower on suppliers’ priority lists.

Gastwirth said he expects higher component costs to translate into fewer consumer products and increased prices as memory can account for roughly 30% of a product’s bill of materials, making shortages particularly painful for consumer device makers.

Both analysts agree that AI customers will continue receiving preferential treatment as long as supply remains constrained. Howard estimates that AI-related applications could account for as much as 75% of total DRAM revenue within a few years.

Howard and Gastwirth aren’t the only analysts singing from the same songbook.

According to a recently published report by Dell’Oro Group, worldwide data center IT semiconductor and component revenue for servers and storage systems surged 182% in the second quarter of 2026, with DRAM and storage revenue growing at a triple-digit pace, as average selling prices per bit more than doubled year over year. Accelerated server deployments also drove strong demand for complementary components, including HBM, CPUs, memory, and high-speed back-end NICs.

Omdia has also raised its 2026 semiconductor revenue forecast to 94.1% year-over-year growth, driven by unprecedented demand for DRAM as AI infrastructure investment continues to outpace global supply, with memory ICs now expected to account for more than 50% of total semiconductor revenue in 2026.

The research firm said AI demand has exceeded the industry’s current ability to produce and package chips, with bottlenecks across HBM, advanced packaging, and node capacity expected to persist until at least 2027.

India’s electronics ecosystem is assembling itself like a puzzle, with stubborn pieces trying to find their place—some already locked in, many still being cut to shape.

When S. Krishnan, secretary of the Indian Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, called 2026 a “landmark year” for semiconductors, he wasn’t pointing only to the ₹1.275 trillion (~$13.25 billion) outlay under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0). He was also pointing to three semiconductor packaging facilities set up by Micron, Kaynes, and CG Semi in Sanand, Gujarat, which began commercial production in the first half of 2026—proof that some pieces have already clicked into place. However, locking a piece in place doesn’t mean the puzzle is solved. These packaging units run on legacy processes—the harder climb toward flip-chip, 2.5D, and DRAM packaging is still ahead.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi framed the ambition in sweeping terms at the inauguration of CG Semi’s commercial production: “Our aim is to develop the entire ecosystem in India, from chip design to fabrication to packaging. … India’s youth will drive the next technological revolution—in AI, robotics, and next-gen tech—powered by Made in India chips.”

It’s a compelling vision, but most of the equipment and specialty chemicals feeding India’s electronics and semiconductor ecosystem are still imported. That remains a structural vulnerability that undercuts the “self-reliance” messaging until the upstream capabilities—materials, equipment, and process technology—that ISM 2.0 promises are actually built.

That’s precisely where the smaller, sharper pieces—India’s deep-tech startups—earn their place. Vimag Labs is building a wirelessly excited motor that needs no rare-Earth magnets. NoPo Technologies is scaling single-walled carbon nanotube production for electronics and energy storage, building what it claims will be the world’s second-largest such plant in Bengaluru and going head-to-head with established global manufacturers.

If you think the puzzle ends at motors and materials, take a breath: India is also reaching for compute itself. Amith Singhee, CTO of IBM India and South Asia, walked through the company’s planned Quantum System Two installation in Amaravati, which is set to put a production-grade quantum computer within reach of Indian researchers. Meanwhile, researchers at IIT Bombay and IISc Bangalore are working on neuromorphic chips wired to think the way brains do.

In this Special Report, EE Times lays out every piece as it’s cut and placed—the packaging plants racing toward advanced nodes, the startups rewriting India’s supply chain, and the labs betting on compute architectures the world hasn’t commercialized yet.
